Topic covered: Foundations
What I Did:
Plotted time series plots for discrete and continuous time series data: Section 1
What I Learned:
A time series is an ordered sequence of observations collected over time. The ordering matters since observations are often dependent on previous observations (sequential correlation).






Assumption



Equally spaced measurements.








Assumption



Autocorrelation across time.


A time series is a single measurement taken at multiple points through time to give a series of measurements through time.
Noise (stochastic) in data introduces different realisations. An observed time series is only one realisation of an underlying stochastic process. This is important as we are not just trying to model the observations but the process that generated them.
Questions:
Q: How does noise introduce different realisations?
A: In normal regression the pattern is fixed and the noise sits on top of it
\[
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + e_i,
\] where each error term is independent.
In an AR process the noise actually builds the pattern. This means that every apparent trend is made of past shocks that haven’t died away yet. A different set of shocks will give a different shape because the shape of the path comes from noise. It isn’t that time series errors are correlated but that each observation is a weighted sum of every past shock making observations correlated.

set.seed(1)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (i in 1:6) plot(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.9), n = 100), main = paste("Realisation", i), ylab = "y")

Lecture 2
Date: 3 August 2026
Topic covered: The Forecasting Problem
What I Did:
Looked at stationary AR processes: Section 1
What I Learned:
A forecast horizon is how far into the future you try to predict values. When looking at time series data we are looking for stable, informative patterns (not just a lot of data).






Forecasting vs Goal setting vs Planning



A forecast is a prediction about what will happen in the future based on evidence that we have (with some uncertainty). Goal setting is what we want to happen in the future and planning is how we reach our goal.


The uncertainty associated with forecasting gives rise to forecast intervals (not just point estimates).
A random walk is a process where memory is permanent. Every future shock accumulates endlessly resulting in forecast variance growing linearly. A stationary AR is a process where memory decays geometrically. Shocks die out, forcing the forecast back to the process mean.
Questions:
Q: If a process changes over time, at what point can we discard previous observations when forecasting?
A: This is decided by the model and is called the model’s memory. A mean benchmark will use every observation and just forecast the mean, the naive benchmark will use the most recent observation, exponential smoothing uses all observations but weights them differently (older observations are given less weight). You would also discard observations if a structural break occurs.






Note



When determining the number of observations to estimate the model (training set) more is usually better, unless the process has changed.

Lecture 3
Date: 17 August 2026
Topics covered: Exploring a Series, Benchmarks and Forecast Accuracy
What I Did:
Worked through Time Series Analysis in R using the AirPassengers dataset: Section 1
What I Learned:
Time domain looks at previous observations whereas the frequency domain looks at previous cycles. Often you will need to look at both of these domains.






Trend vs Seasonality vs Cycles



A trend is the long-run direction of movement in a time series. Seasonality models a pattern that repeats itself at a fixed AND known interval. A cycle is a long oscillation where the length is NOT fixed.


When dealing with time series data you may encounter changing variability. Here you need to transform the data to stabilise variance and difference to remove trend anf seasonality. When structural breaks are present in the data you can either use an indicator variable at the break or you can fit separate models on either side of the break.
There are 4 benchmark forecasting models: Mean, Naive, Seasonal naive and Drift.






Residuals are not forecast errors



Residuals are for diagnostics; forecast errors are for evaluation!


You cannot run normal cross-validation on time series data since the ordering of observations matters. Future observations must never be used when estimating a forecasting model.
Questions:
Q: How do you identify a significant structural break?
A: This can be done using formal tests, dependent on whether the date of the break is known prior to looking at the data. If the date is known in advance, if there was a policy change, you can use Chow’s test. Chow’s test fits the model before and after the date of the break and uses an F-test to check if there is a statistically significant difference in model parameters. If the date is unknown you can run a Chow test at every possible date and take the largest F, compared against adjusted critical values. This is a sup-F test and accounts for having searched over every date, making it harder to declare a break.

Since you can’t perform regular cross-validation on time series data you use a different approach. Walk-forward validation advances the forecast origin one step at a time and re-estimates the model at each step. Expanding window validation keeps every historical observation while moving the forecast origin forward. Sliding window validation keeps the training window length fixed while moving the forecast origin forward.
Expanding window is good for stable processes whereas sliding window is good for rapidly changing processes.

Lecture 5
Date: 24 August 2026
Topic covered: Linear Models for the Conditional Mean
What I Did:
Fit both ARIMA and SARIMA to the AirPassengers dataset:Section 1
What I Learned:
The moving average, MA(\(q\)), model is driven by lagged shocks. The dependence is based on errors not actual observations. The model has short memory. An MA(\(q\)) is always stationary is restricted to be invertible.
The autoregressive, AR(\(p\)), model regresses a series on its own path.
ARMA combines both MA and AR models and is fitted by maximum likelihood, not OLS, since the past chocks are never observed.






Note



ACF and PACF graphs are used to determine which ARMA model to fit. An AR(\(p\)) has a PACF that cuts off after lag \(p\). An MA(\(q\)) has an ACF that cuts off after lag \(q\).


The ARIMA(\(p,d,q\)) model allows for differencing and the SARIMA model includes seasonality.
Questions:
Q: How can you determine if there is additional seasonality in a dataset after differencing or if it is just noise? For example in Section 1, there were still spikes at some lags in the PACF after log-transforming and differencing the AirPassengers dataset.
A: You can check if the residuals look like white noise by using a Ljung-Box test. A non-significant test means that there is no remaining proof of autocorrelation (even if there are will a few lags that spike in the ACF/PACF).

Additional Lecture 1 with Sulaiman
Date: 16 September 2026
Topic covered: Conditional Variance Models (ARCH and GARCH)
What I Did:
Worked through the provided Lab: Section 1
What I Learned:
All previous models have simply modelled the conditional mean and assumed constant variance. This fails for financial return data as it understates risk during periods where risk is highest and overstates risk when it is lowest. We now have both a mean (predictable component of the series) and a variance (conditional variance) equation.






Note



A series can be uncorrelated and still highly predictable in magnitude.


The ARCH model specifies conditional variance as a function of past squared innovations. The simplest case being \(\sigma^2_t = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2\).






Volatility clustering



Large changes tend to follow large changes and small changes tend to follow small changes. Returns are often uncorrelated, hence why the ACF of returns indicates very little, however squared returns can be strongly autocorrelated.


The GARCH model includes the previous variance to the ARCH equation. This makes it equivalent to an ARCH model with infinite memory. a GARCH(1,1) model is usually sufficient in practice.
\[
\sigma_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta_1 \sigma_{t-1}^2,
\] where \(\alpha_1\) measures how strongly volatility reacts to a new shock, \(\beta_1\) measures how long that reaction lasts, \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1\) is the persistence.
Questions:
Q: Why must \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1 < 1\)?
A: When \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1 < 1\) this ensures that the long-run variance is \(\bar{\sigma}^2 = \frac{\alpha_0}{1- \alpha_1 - \beta_1}\) and that the process has a benchmark variance for the volatility to return to. When \(\alpha_1 + \beta_1 = 1\) (IGARCH) the shocks to volatility are permanent. This means that all the weight is on the past and none is on the long-run level. This is the variance equivalent of a random walk.

Lecture 7
Date: 14 September 2026
Topic covered: Exponential Smoothing
What I Did:
Worked through Exponential Smoothing Exercises: Section 2
What I Learned:
Exponential smoothing forecasts are weighted averages of past observations. Weights decrease exponentially the further back in time you go. The smoothing parameter \(\alpha\) adjusts the weight put on past observations. A large \(\alpha\) puts a lot of weight on the most recent observation, similar to the Naive forecast. A small \(\alpha\) averages over a long history, similar to the Mean forecast. This is similar to GARCH but applied to observations instead of squared shocks.






SES vs Holt vs Holt-Winters



Simple exponential smoothing (SES) only updates a level resulting in flat forecasts. Holt’s method adds a trend equation, that describes the slope, so forecasts follow a straight line. Holt-Winters adds a seasonal equation. Each component gets its own smoothing parameter (\(\alpha\), \(\beta\), \(\gamma\)).


The smoothing parameters and initial states (\(\ell_0\), \(b_0\)) are estimated by minimising the sum of squared one-step-ahead errors. Fitted values are one-step-ahead forecasts, so residuals are always one-step-ahead errors.
To turn the exponential smoothing algorithm into a state-space model we can write it in error-corrected form: \(y_t = \ell_{t-1} + e_t\), \(\ell_t = \ell_{t-1} + \alpha e_t\). This allows us to estimate \(\sigma\) and build prediction intervals.
This is what ets() does.






Prediction intervals are usually too narrow



Standard prediction intervals only capture the random error and ignore the uncertainty in parameter estimates and choice of model.


Questions:
Q: How do we get variances of SES forecasts (\(\sigma^2[1+\alpha^2(h-1)]\)) if the point forecasts are flat?
A: The point forecast stays at \(\ell_T\), but every future error also moves the level by \(\alpha e_t\). These shifts add up, so uncertainty grows linearly with \(h\) even though the mean does not change.

Date: 21 September 2026
Topic covered: Time Series Regression Models
What I Did:
Worked through Chapter 2: Time Series Regression Models and the provided slides, rerunning the R code that had been included. Used a Kalman filter to estimate regression coefficients in the US consumption example: Section 2
What I Learned:
Time Series Regression includes explanatory variables in time series models. This allows one to include trend and seasonality covariates in the model instead of just differencing the series to make it stationary.






ARMAX vs regression with ARMA errors



ARMAX includes lagged values of the response as predictors, \(y_t = \beta x_t + \phi y_{t-1} + \dots\). This means that \(\beta\) can no longer be interpreted as the effect of \(x\) on the mean of \(y\). Regression with ARMA errors keeps the normal regression equation and lets the errors follow an ARMA process, \(y_t = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_t + \eta_t\). This means that \(\beta_1\) can still be interpreted in the usual way.


Harmonic regression assumes that the seasonal pattern stays the same over time.






Autocorrelated errors



When errors are autocorrelated, OLS still gives unbiased estimates but they are no longer efficient. This means that the standard errors, tests and intervals are also wrong.
This can be fixed with generalised least squares by using gls() with corAR1() or corARMA() or with arima(..., xreg = ).

Lecture 9
Date: 28 September 2026
Topic covered: State-Space Models
What I Did:
Worked through the dlm practical and the State Space and Kalman Filter tutorial: Section 2
What I Learned:
A state-space model has both an observation equation and a state equation.
The observation equation \(y_t = F\theta_t + v_t\) links what we observe to an unobserved state whereas the state equation \(\theta_t = G\theta_{t-1} + w_t\) describes how the state changes over time.






Note



Regression, ARIMA and exponential smoothing models can all be written in state-space form. State-space models don’t need stationarity since trend and seasonality are modelled directly and allowed to change over time.


The Kalman filter is a recursive algorithm that first predicts and then updates. First the state, \(a_t, R_t\), and the next observation, \(f_t, Q_t\), are predicted. Then the state estimate, \(m_t, C_t\), is updated. The updated estimate is a weighted average of the prediction and the new observation where the Kalman gain decides how much weight is assigned to the observation.






Bayesian Framework



The Kalman filter works in a Bayesian way where, \(\text{posterior} \propto \text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}\). The posterior becomes the prior of the next step.

Lecture 10
Date: 5 October 2026
Topic covered: Kalman Filter
What I Did:
Continued working through the dlm practical and the State Space and Kalman Filter tutorial: Section 2
What I Learned:
The Kalman filter is used to filter and forecast in dynamic linear Gaussian systems. This filter is recursive so we can process new observations as they arrive. The Kalman smoother starts at the end of a series and works backwards. This is better for looking backwards (not prediction).






Filtering vs Smoothing vs Forecasting



If we estimate the state at time \(t\) using data up to time \(s\):

\(s < t\) = forecasting
\(s = t\) = filtering
\(s > t\) = smoothing



Forecasting and filtering are done using the Kalman filter. Smoothing is done using the Kalman smoother.
The likelihood is the product of one-step-ahead predictive densities, \(y_t \mid y_{1:t-1} \sim N(f_t, Q_t)\). The unknown variances, \(V\) and \(W\), can be estimated by maximum likelihood.
Prediction intervals use \(Q_t = FR_tF' + V\). They are prediction intervals (not confidence intervals) because they are for a future observation and include the observation noise, \(V\), as well as the uncertainty about the state.
If there are missing observations present in the data, there is nothing to update with and the Kalman gain will be zero. Consecutive missing observations increase uncertainty.






Method (conceptual)




The prior predicts the next state from the previous estimate of the state, with some uncertainty (state equation).
The likelihood asks how likely the new observation is given all possible states (observation equation).
The new posterior, for the current state, is given by combining the likelihood and the prior



Questions:
Q: Why does the Kalman filter only work for linear Gaussian state-space models?
A: The Kalman filter does a linear transformation of a Gaussian which gives another Gaussian.
\[
\text{Gaussian prior} \times \text{Gaussian likelihood} \propto \text{Gaussian posterior}
\] The Kalman filter only keeps track of the mean and variance. When we have a non-linear or non-Gaussian distribution we either end up with a skewed distribution or a posterior with no closed form.

Learning outcomes

Explain what a time series is and how it differs from cross-sectional data, and say why temporal dependence calls for its own methods.
Treat an observed series as one realisation of a stochastic process.
Explain what forecasting is, judge when a process is predictable, and keep forecasts, goals and plans separate.

Identify trend, seasonality, cycle and irregular variation in a plot, and describe the shapes each of them takes in practice.
Produce the four benchmark forecasts, and evaluate any competing model against them on data it has not seen.
Use the lag and lead operators, and the algebra built on them, to write models compactly.
Define weak stationarity, say which of its conditions a given series violates, and choose a transformation that restores it.
Define white noise, MA, AR, ARMA, ARIMA and SARIMA processes, derive their basic properties, and identify them from an ACF and a PACF.
Fit, diagnose and forecast these models in R, following the workflow of Box and Jenkins, and test residuals against the white noise standard.
Explain volatility clustering and fit ARCH and GARCH models to it


What is a time series?
Time series is a single measurement taken at multiple points across time. Technically we are modelling the same thing over and over again (this makes sense as to why there is sequential correlation).






Note



Time series model dependence through sequential observations.








Assumption



Equally spaced measurements.








Assumption



Autocorrelation across time.




Qualitative, Continuous and Discrete Series
Example: Continuous series





Figure 1: Time series plot of the number of monthly airline passengers from 1949 to 1960.




Figure 1 plots the number of monthly airline passengers over a 12 year period. This figure clearly illustrates the concepts of seasonality and trend.
Example: Discrete series





Figure 2: Time series plot of the number of seals from 1975 to 1999.




Figure 2 plots the changing number of observed seals over a period of 25 years.
What to do when you have missing observations in a time series?
In discrete time series to deal with missing observations you can express the model in state-space form (ARIMA or Structural Time Series). For a missing observation \(y_t\), skip the update step in the kalman filter and only run the prediction step. The likelihood is evaluated only over the observed time points.






Kalman filtering



Kalman filtering (linear quadratic estimation) is an algorithm that uses a series of measurements over time to estimate unknown variables, by estimating a joint probability distribution over the variables for each time-step.


In continuous time series, missing observations look like irregularly spaced sampling intervals. You can model the underlying system using Stochastic Differential Equations (CARMA) or you can aggregate the irregular time steps into regular, discrete intervals.


Temporal granularity and the aggregation effect
Aggregating up can either smooth out high-frequency structure (stock returns, etc) or can reveal low-frequency structure (Sales, etc).


One realisation of a stochastic process
Noise in the data introduces different realisations. If your model fits one dataset perfectly then it is overfitting.

Exploratory Data Analysis
The duplicate observation in the Dam_Levels_from_2000 dataset was removed by retaining only the first occurrence of each date. The dam level series contained only 1 missing value that was left as NA.





Figure 13: Theewaterskloof dam capacity from January 2000 to January 2026.









Figure 14: Average Pacific sea surface temperature from January 2000 to April 2026.




Both Figure 13 and Figure 14 show that these series are noisy. The dam levels data has multiple year drops and slow recoveries whereas the the SST oscillates more uniformly around its mean. The daily data is aggregated to monthly averages to obtain a clearer visualisation of the seasonality present in the data and to smooth out high frequency noise.





Figure 15: Theewaterskloof dam capacity from January 2000 to January 2026.









Figure 16: Average Pacific sea surface temperature from January 2000 to April 2026.




As seen in Figure 15 and Figure 16, both datasets display strong 12-month seasonal patterns. The dam level data also has an irregular drought/recovery cycle that appears to follows the hydrological cycle.
Both the Dam_Levels_from_2000 dataset and the sst dataset have observations from 2000 to 2026. The SST series has two periods of missing observations, November 2021 to March 2023 and October 2024 to March 2025, due to the bouy array not recording. These gaps cannot be reliable smoothed over and have been left as missing observations.
Southern Africa experienced severe droughts between 2015 and 2018. In the figures below, dam capacity across this period is compared with lagged SST, approximately 3 months earlier.





Figure 17: Theewaterskloof dam capacity for 2015 to 2019 and sea surface temperature from 3 months earlier.




In Figure 17, dam capacity declines to reach a minimum around 2018 and then recovers into 2020. The SST series has missing values for March and April 2017 but still shows a slightly elevated double peak in both 2015 and 2016. This is consistent with the El Nino that occurred during that period. Both series maintain their strong seasonal patterns, however it is difficult to determine the lagged relationship.





Figure 18: Deseasonalised dam capacity from 2015 to 2019 and sea surface temperature from 3 months earlier.




Figure 18 re-illustrates the cycle identified in Figure 17. With the seasonality of the series removed, dam capacity decreases smoothly to a minimum around 2018 and recovers steadily through 2019. Rising SST in the deseasonalised plot precedes the decreased dam capacity during the 2015 to 2016 period, however during the 2018 to 2019 recovery phase, SST is rising. This suggests that the relationship between dam capacity and SST is not a stable relationship across the whole period and that other drivers are likely contributing to the dam level recovery.





Figure 19: Monthly trends in Theewaterskloof dam capacity and average Pacific sea surface temperature from 2000 to 2026. The blue line in each panel indicates the mean for that month.




Figure 19 illustrates the strong seasonal pattern already identified in Figure 15 and Figure 16. Dam levels reach a minimum around May and peak in September. The variation in dam levels within the months is approximately the same across all months. SST peaks in April and is lowest in September. Unlike the dam levels, the months with lower temperatures experience greater variability in the recorded temperatures compared to months where the temperature is higher. Dam capacity (%) and SST (°C) are measured on different scales. This means that the two series’ overall variability cannot be directly compared. It is worth noting that the structural gaps present in the sea surface temperature series result in some months having more observations than others.





Figure 20: ACF and PACF plots for Theewaterskloof dam capacity.









Figure 21: ACF and PACF plots for Pacific sea surface temperature.




Both Figure 20 and Figure 21 indicate that these time series are non-stationary. The ACF of the sea surface temperature illustrates a regular seasonal pattern with sharp peaks occurring at regular intervals compared to the ACF of dam levels which has a less stable seasonal pattern seen by the less regularly-spaced peaks. This suggests that the dam level pattern is influenced by a long-term irregular hydrological cycle as opposed to the seasonal rainfall pattern alone. Both PACF plots have a large spike at lag 1. This is typical of a non-stationary process. The dam level PACF plot has a large negative spike at lag 2, indicative of an AR(2) process. This is followed by a few significant positive spiked that indicate a further short-run structure. The SST PACF plot has the same pattern as the dam levels PACF plot, with a large positive spike at lag 1 followed by a large negative spike at lag 2. There is also a second series of significant positive spikes from lag 7 to 10. The order selection for the AR and SARIMA models is based on the ACF and PACF plots of the seasonally differenced series.





Figure 22: Decomposition of Theewaterskloof dam capacity series.









Figure 23: Decomposition of average Pacific sea surface temperature series from 2000 to 2026.




Figure 23 plots the decomposition of the sea surface temperature series. There are missing observations from November 2021 to March 2023 and October 2024 to March 2025. These observations have been interpolated, not observed, for completeness of the decomposition across the entire series and should not be interpreted as true measurements.
As seen in Figure 22 and Figure 23, both the dam level and sea surface temperature series show strong seasonal trends with Figure 22 showing multi-year drought and recovery cycles. There are noticeable dips in 2005 and, more severely, 2018, as opposed to a stable long-run trend. The SST trend is more stable than the dam trend for majority of the observed period. This can be attributed to SST being driven by the annual warming and cooling due to heating angles whereas dam levels are driven not only by seasonal patterns but also by the long-term irregular hydrological cycle. Towards the end of the SST series there is a sharp drop followed by a steep increase, this is consistent with the predicted 2026/2027 El Nino even but should be interpreted carefully.

Model fitting
This project fits and compares AR,MA,ARMA,ARIMA and SARIMA against the benchmark models: Mean, Naive, Seasonal naive and Drift, for both the Dam_Levels_from_2000 and sst datasets. A time series regression model is then fit on Dam_Levels_from_2000 using the sea surface temperature as a predictor to determine if sea surface temperature in the eastern Pacific can improve the prediciton of Theewaterskloof dam levels to aid in drought prediction.





Figure 24: ACF and PACF plots for both dam levels and sea surface temperature for the seasonally differenced data.




Figure 24 shows the ACF and PACF of both the dam level and SST series after seasonal differencing. The dam level ACF decays monotonically from lag 1. The PACF has significant spikes at lags 1 and 2, this is consistent with the AR(2) structure identified in the EDA. There are some significant spikes at lags 12-14 which is more indicative of a seasonal MA term than a seasonal AR term. The SST PACF is noisier than the dam level one, with a few additional significant spikes. This irregular autocorrelation structure provides evidence that SST does not reduce to a low-order SARIMA model.
Dam level data are available from 2000 to 2026. The most recent 2 years are held out as a test set and the remainder is used as the training set. SST uses the clean pre-2021 subset as the training set with the last two years, 2020-2021 as the test set.

title: Predicting drought in the Western Cape
text:
This project fits and compares autoregressive models (AR, MA, ARMA, SARIMA) to the Theewaterskloof dam level and eastern Pacific sea surface temperature (SST) individually. SST is then included as a covariate in a SARIMAX model to determine if it can be used to improve dam level forecasts.
Section & Topic: Autoregressive Models
Project Type: Model implementation
Aim: Are the sea surface temperature in the eastern Pacific Ocean and the Theewaterskloof dam levels predictable?
Data Used:
[https://www.pmel.noaa.gov/tao/drupal/disdel/] [https://odp-cctegis.opendata.arcgis.com/]
Methods Used: AR, MA, ARMA, SARIMA, SARIMAX (dynamic regression with sea surface temperature as a predictor), compared against Mean, Naive, Seasonal naive and Drift benchmarks.
The aim of this project is to use autoregressive models to forecast Theewaterskloof Dam levels and eastern Pacific sea surface temperature (along 95W), individually, as well as using SST as a lagged predictor to try and improve dam-level forecasts. This project will be used to test the hypothesis that eastern Pacific SST can be used as a leading indicator of drought risk in the Western Cape.
The El Niño phase of the El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) is characterised by anomalous warming of sea surface temperatures in the eastern and central Pacific Ocean. This phenomenon typically starts between March and June, reaching its peak around the following December/January (Mason, 2001). An El Niño event typically causes warm and dry conditions over Southern Africa, with effects emerging within the year following the El Niño onset in the Pacific (Thomson et al., 2003). Over the 2015-2016 season, Southern Africa experienced severe drought with the 2015/2016 El Niño being identified as a contributing factor. This saw a drop in dam levels and severe water restrictions being implemented.
The South African Weather Service (SAWS) is warning against a super El Niño event in 2026-2027, as current sea surface temperatures rise beyond the threshold used to define a very strong El Niño (Mail & Guardian, 2026).
This project focuses on Theewaterskloof Dam, the single largest reservoir in the Western Cape Water Supply System.









Detailed Analysis & Code Script[cite: 1]




The duplicate observation in the Dam_Levels_from_2000 dataset was removed by retaining only the first occurrence of each date. The dam level series contained only 1 missing value that was left as NA.





Figure 1: Theewaterskloof dam capacity from January 2000 to January 2026.









Figure 2: Average eastern Pacific sea surface temperature from January 2000 to April 2026.




Both Figure 1 and Figure 2 show that these series are noisy. The dam levels data has multiple year drops and slow recoveries whereas the SST oscillates more uniformly around its mean. The daily data is aggregated to monthly averages to obtain a clearer visualisation of the seasonality present in the data and to smooth out high frequency noise.





Figure 3: Theewaterskloof dam capacity from January 2000 to January 2026.









Figure 4: Average eastern Pacific sea surface temperature from January 2000 to April 2026.




As seen in Figure 3 and Figure 4, both datasets display strong 12-month seasonal patterns. The dam level data also has an irregular drought/recovery cycle that appears to follow the hydrological cycle.
Both the Dam_Levels_from_2000 dataset and the sst dataset have observations from 2000 to 2026. The SST series has two periods of missing observations, November 2021 to March 2023 and October 2024 to March 2025, due to the buoy array not recording. These gaps cannot be reliable smoothed over and have been left as missing observations.
Southern Africa experienced a severe drought between 2015 and 2018. In the figures below, dam capacity across this period is compared with lagged SST, approximately 3 months earlier.





Figure 5: Theewaterskloof dam capacity from 2015 to 2019 with sea surface temperature from 3 months earlier.




In Figure 5, dam capacity declines to reach a minimum around 2018 and then recovers through 2019. The SST series has missing values for March and April 2017 but still shows a slightly elevated double peak in both 2015 and 2016. This is consistent with the El Niñothat occurred during that period. Both series maintain their strong seasonal patterns, however it is difficult to determine the lagged relationship.





Figure 6: Deseasonalised dam capacity from 2015 to 2019 with sea surface temperature from 3 months earlier.




Figure 6 re-illustrates the cycle identified in Figure 5. With the seasonality of the series removed, dam capacity decreases smoothly to a minimum around 2018 and recovers steadily through 2019. Rising SST in the deseasonalised plot precedes the decreased dam capacity during the 2015 to 2016 period, however during the 2018 to 2019 recovery phase, SST is rising. This suggests that the relationship between dam capacity and SST is not a stable relationship across the whole period and that other drivers are likely contributing to the dam level recovery.





Figure 7: Monthly trends in Theewaterskloof dam capacity and average Pacific sea surface temperature from 2000 to 2026. The blue line in each panel indicates the mean for that month.




Figure 7 illustrates the strong seasonal pattern already identified in Figure 3 and Figure 4. Dam levels reach a minimum around May and peak in September. The variation in dam levels within the months is approximately the same across all months. SST peaks in April and is lowest in September. Unlike the dam levels, the months with lower temperatures experience greater variability in the recorded temperatures compared to months where the temperature is higher. Dam capacity (%) and SST (°C) are measured on different scales. This means that the two series’ overall variability cannot be directly compared. It is worth noting that the structural gaps present in the sea surface temperature series result in some months having more observations than others.





Figure 8: ACF and PACF plots for Theewaterskloof dam capacity.









Figure 9: ACF and PACF plots for eastern Pacific sea surface temperature.




Both Figure 8 and Figure 9 indicate that these time series are non-stationary. The ACF of the sea surface temperature illustrates a regular seasonal pattern with sharp peaks occurring at regular intervals compared to the ACF of dam levels which has a less stable seasonal pattern seen by the less regularly-spaced peaks. This suggests that the dam level pattern is influenced by a long-term irregular hydrological cycle as opposed to the seasonal rainfall pattern alone. Both PACF plots have a large spike at lag 1. This is typical of a non-stationary process. The dam level PACF plot has a large negative spike at lag 2, indicative of an AR(2) process. This is followed by a few significant positive spikes that indicate a further short-run structure. The SST PACF plot has the same pattern as the dam levels PACF plot, with a large positive spike at lag 1 followed by a large negative spike at lag 2. There is also a second series of significant positive spikes from lag 7 to 10. The order selection for the AR and SARIMA models is based on the ACF and PACF plots of the seasonally differenced series.





Figure 10: Decomposition of Theewaterskloof dam capacity series from 2000 to 2026.









Figure 11: Decomposition of eastern Pacific sea surface temperature series from 2000 to 2026.




Figure 11 plots the decomposition of the sea surface temperature series. There are missing observations from November 2021 to March 2023 and October 2024 to March 2025. These observations have been interpolated, not observed, for completeness of the decomposition across the entire series and should not be interpreted as true measurements.
As seen in Figure 10 and Figure 11, both the dam level and sea surface temperature series show strong seasonal trends with Figure 10 showing multi-year drought and recovery cycles. There are noticeable dips in 2005 and, more severely, 2018, as opposed to a stable long-run trend. The SST trend is more stable than the dam trend for majority of the observed period. This can be attributed to SST being driven by the annual warming and cooling due to heating angles whereas dam levels are driven not only by seasonal patterns but also by the long-term irregular hydrological cycle. Towards the end of the SST series there is a sharp drop followed by a steep increase, this is consistent with the predicted 2026/2027 El Niñoeven but should be interpreted carefully.



This project fits and compares AR,MA,ARMA and SARIMA against the benchmark models: Mean, Naive, Seasonal naive and Drift, for both the Dam_Levels_from_2000 and sst datasets. A time series regression model is then fit on Dam_Levels_from_2000 using the sea surface temperature as a predictor to determine if sea surface temperature in the eastern Pacific can improve the prediction of Theewaterskloof dam levels to aid in drought prediction.





Figure 12: ACF and PACF plots for both dam levels and sea surface temperature for the seasonally differenced data.




Figure 12 shows the ACF and PACF of both the dam level and SST series after seasonal differencing. The dam level ACF decays monotonically from lag 1. The PACF has significant spikes at lags 1 and 2, this is consistent with the AR(2) structure identified in the EDA. There are some significant spikes at lags 12-14 which is more indicative of a seasonal MA term than a seasonal AR term. The SST PACF is noisier than the dam level one, with a few additional significant spikes. This irregular autocorrelation structure provides evidence that SST does not reduce to a low-order SARIMA model.


Dam level data are available from 2000 to 2026. The most recent 2 years are held out as a test set and the remainder is used as the training set. SST uses the clean pre-2021 dataset with the last two years, 2020-2021 as the test set and the previous years as the training set.

The above fitted models model the dam level and SST independently. Next, a dynamic regression (SARIMAX) model is fitted using lagged SST as a predictor of dam levels. This is done to try and achieve the projects aim of predicting drought in the Western cape using eastern Pacific sea surface temperature.





Figure 13: Cross-correlation between dam capacity and sea surface temperature.




The CCF in Figure 13 oscillates with approximately a 12 month period. This is seen by the troughs at -24,-12,0,12 and 24 and peaks at -18,-6,6 and 18. This illustrates the seasonal pattern already observed in Figure 3 and Figure 4 and does not necessarily indicate a clean lead-lag relationship. Considering the lags for where SST precedes dam levels, the strongest correlation is at lag 6. This is used as the optimal lag in the SARIMAX model.

This is expected since the lagged SST added no improved prediction accuracy in the linear regression model when the errors were modelled with SARIMA. Although the error values for the benchmark linear model are on average the lowest out of all models, this is misleading. Figure 14 showed clear autocorrelated residuals and thus the model is not correctly modelling a genuine predictive relationship but rather a short-run overlap due to both dam levels and SST sharing an upward trend from 2018 to 2019 (Figure 6). This provides no evidence that eastern Pacific sea surface temperatures improve dam level forecasts more than what the series history does.











Figure 16: 2-year forecasts of Theewaterskloof dam capacity using a SARIMA(2,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] model.




Figure 16 shows the forecast using SARIMA(2,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] on the dam levels series through 2026 and 2027. The strong seasonal cycle is maintained although the forecasted peaks are slightly lower than the previous few years. The model is reverting back towards more typical levels as opposed to just extrapolating the most recent observations. The uncertainty associated with these forecasts grows substantially with the forecast horizon. Since this model is built on its own history with no covariate added it cannot predict the onset of an El Niñoevent nor drought in the Western Cape.








Figure 17: 2-year forecasts of eastern Pacific sea surface temperature using an AR(1,0,0)(0,1,0)[12] model.




Figure 17 shows the forecast using AR(1,0,0)(0,1,0)[12] on the sea surface temperature series through 2022 and 2023. The series maintains its strong seasonal pattern with temperatures peaking around 26°C and dropping to approximately 22°C. This is similar to the historical pattern. Uncertainty in the prediction intervals grows with the forecast horizon but not as much as for the dam level series. The prediction only extends into 2023 since the model was built on pre-2021 data due to large portions of missing observations after 2021. A simple AR process is unable to predict unprecedented events as the model forecasts revert towards typical seasonal values. Even if the model was forecasting into 2027 it would be unable to pick up the anticipated 2026/2027 El Niñoevent.






The optimal model for the Theewaterskloof dam capacity series is the SARIMA(2,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] model. This model was selected based on the PACF plot in Figure 12 as well as a comparison of its error metrics with the initial SARIMA model specification. For sea surface temperature, Figure 12’s PACF plot suggested that SST prediction would not be improved by a more complex seasonal model. This was confirmed when the AR(1,0,0)(0,1,0)[12] model, on average, outperformed all other candidate models, when their error metrics were compared. Using SST as a lagged predictor for dam capacity was statistically insignificant as it did not improve predictive accuracy beyond what the series history already did.



There were several limitations when working with these datasets. The structural gaps present in the SST series (November 2021 - March 2023, October 2024 - March 2025) meant that the regression analysis could only use pre-2021 data. This loss of information decreased the size of the training set and meant that the model could not predict into 2027, when the super El Niñois anticipated.
The CCF-derived 6 month lag is consistent with the typical literature-motivated 3-6 month window for El Nino, however, the CCF is dominated by the common 12-month seasonality of both the series rather than a clean lead-lag signal. Thus, it cannot be accurately determined if a 6 month lag is the true lag.



To predict drought in the Western Cape, it would be more useful to use rainfall data as this has a direct impact on dam levels. Monitoring water usage across the country may also provide improved predictive information that eastern Pacific sea surface temperature.
The structural gaps in the SST data could be worked around by using a more comprehensive set of buoy observations that span a wider longitudinal range than the single 95W array used here. By replacing the buoy array with an array that averages over a larger region of the Pacific, there would be fewer missing observations and the series would not need to be truncated to avoid large structural gaps. The El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) moves through El Nino, La Niña and neutral periods. It may be useful to use a regime-switching model that would capture this variability as opposed to a model with fixed coefficients.

Figure 7: Monthly trends in Theewaterskloof dam capacity and average Pacific sea surface temperature from 2000 to 2026. The blue line in each panel indicates the mean for that month.




Figure 7 illustrates the strong seasonal pattern already identified in Figure 3 and Figure 4. Dam levels reach a minimum around May and peak in September. The variation in dam levels within the months is approximately the same across all months. SST peaks in April and is lowest in September. Unlike the dam levels, the months with lower temperatures experience greater variability in the recorded temperatures compared to months where the temperature is higher. Dam capacity (%) and SST (°C) are measured on different scales. This means that the two series’ overall variability cannot be directly compared. It is worth noting that the structural gaps present in the sea surface temperature series result in some months having more observations than others.





Figure 8: ACF and PACF plots for Theewaterskloof dam capacity.









Figure 9: ACF and PACF plots for eastern Pacific sea surface temperature.




Both Figure 8 and Figure 9 indicate that these time series are non-stationary. The ACF of the sea surface temperature illustrates a regular seasonal pattern with sharp peaks occurring at regular intervals compared to the ACF of dam levels which has a less stable seasonal pattern seen by the less regularly-spaced peaks. This suggests that the dam level pattern is influenced by a long-term irregular hydrological cycle as opposed to the seasonal rainfall pattern alone. Both PACF plots have a large spike at lag 1. This is typical of a non-stationary process. The dam level PACF plot has a large negative spike at lag 2, indicative of an AR(2) process. This is followed by a few significant positive spikes that indicate a further short-run structure. The SST PACF plot has the same pattern as the dam levels PACF plot, with a large positive spike at lag 1 followed by a large negative spike at lag 2. There is also a second series of significant positive spikes from lag 7 to 10. The order selection for the AR and SARIMA models is based on the ACF and PACF plots of the seasonally differenced series.





Figure 10: Decomposition of Theewaterskloof dam capacity series from 2000 to 2026.









Figure 11: Decomposition of eastern Pacific sea surface temperature series from 2000 to 2026.




Figure 11 plots the decomposition of the sea surface temperature series. There are missing observations from November 2021 to March 2023 and October 2024 to March 2025. These observations have been interpolated, not observed, for completeness of the decomposition across the entire series and should not be interpreted as true measurements.
As seen in Figure 10 and Figure 11, both the dam level and sea surface temperature series show strong seasonal trends with Figure 10 showing multi-year drought and recovery cycles. There are noticeable dips in 2005 and, more severely, 2018, as opposed to a stable long-run trend. The SST trend is more stable than the dam trend for majority of the observed period. This can be attributed to SST being driven by the annual warming and cooling due to heating angles whereas dam levels are driven not only by seasonal patterns but also by the long-term irregular hydrological cycle. Towards the end of the SST series there is a sharp drop followed by a steep increase, this is consistent with the predicted 2026/2027 El Niñoeven but should be interpreted carefully.

This project fits and compares AR,MA,ARMA and SARIMA against the benchmark models: Mean, Naive, Seasonal naive and Drift, for both the Dam_Levels_from_2000 and sst datasets. A time series regression model is then fit on Dam_Levels_from_2000 using the sea surface temperature as a predictor to determine if sea surface temperature in the eastern Pacific can improve the prediction of Theewaterskloof dam levels to aid in drought prediction.





Figure 12: ACF and PACF plots for both dam levels and sea surface temperature for the seasonally differenced data.




Figure 12 shows the ACF and PACF of both the dam level and SST series after seasonal differencing. The dam level ACF decays monotonically from lag 1. title: Predicting the volatility of daily Johannesburg Stock Exchange All Share Index returns
text:
This project aims to predict the volatility of the JSE All Share Index (ALSI) returns by fitting both ARCH and GARCH models and determining which models yield the best out-of-sample volatility forecasts. These models are compared to the Exponentially Weighted Moving Average (EWMA) benchmark.
Section & Topic: Conditional Variance Models
Project Type: Model implementation and comparison on real-world data. This includes a GARCH(1,1) likelihood from first principles.
Aim: To predict the volatility of JSE ALSI returns and to determine, from the above mentioned models, the optimal one for out-of-sample volatility and Value-at-Risk forecasts.
Data Used:
Gebbie, T. (2020) Daily Sampled South African Market Index Data 1994-2017, University of Cape Town, Dataset, https://doi.org/10.25375/uct.11302325.v1
Methods Used: ARCH, GARCH and GARCH extensions models are fitted to the JSE ALSI returns.
The aim of this project is to use conditional variance models to predict the volatility of the JSE ALSI returns. JSE return risk is not constant with periods of high volatility following periods of high volatility and periods of low volatility following periods of low volatility. Modelling returns with a constant-variance model results in the risk being understated when it is high and overstated when it is low.
ARCH (Engle, 1982) and GARCH (Bollerslev, 1986) models let the current conditional variance depends on recent shocks as well as yesterday’s variance. GJR-GARCH (Glosten et al., 1993) extends the GARCH model to let negative shocks have a larger effect on volatility than positive ones, this is known as the leverage effect.









Detailed Analysis & Code Script[cite: 1]




The financial series used is the daily FTSE/JSE All Share Index total return index \(P_t\) (ticker J203, dividends reinvested) over the period from 30 June 1995 to 3 February 2017. The time index used is “trading day” since weekends are excluded. The daily log returns (%) are modelled,
\[
r_t = 100[lnP_t - lnP_{t-}].
\] Log returns are modelled since asset prices wander and their variance grows without bound. The series consists of 5396 total daily returns. The models are estimated using the training set (July 1995 - December 2012) and evaluated on the test set (January 2013 - February 2017).

In ?@tbl-arch_tests the small p-values provide evidence that the squared residuals are serially correlated and thus the series has time varying conditional variance.



Conditional variance models consist of both a mean and a variance equation:
\[
r_t = \mu_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} D(0,1),
\]
where \(\mu_t=\mu+\phi r_{t-1}\), \(\sigma_t^2\) is the conditional variance and \(D\) is the standard normal or a standardised Student-\(t\) distribution with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom.
In the ARCH model, the conditional variance depends on past squared shocks. The GARCH model lets the conditional variance depend on its own past as well as on past squared shocks. The GJR-GARCH model is a threshold model that captures the asymmetric leverage effect, where negative shocks increase volatility more than positive shocks of the same magnitude.







Model
Conditional variance \(\sigma_t^2\)




ARCH(\(q\))
\(\alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{q}\alpha_i\varepsilon_{t-i}^2\)


GARCH(\(p,q\))
\(\alpha_0 + \sum^q_{i=1} \alpha_i \varepsilon_{t-i}^2 + \sum^p_{j=1} \beta_j \sigma_{t-j}^2\)


GJR-GARCH(\(p,q\))
\(\alpha_0 + \sum^q_{i=1} (\alpha_i + \gamma_iI_{t-i})\varepsilon^2_{t-i} + \sum^p_{j=1}\beta_j \sigma_{t-j}^2\), where \(I_{t-i} = 1\) if \(\varepsilon_{t-i} < 0\) and \(0\) otherwise



with \(\alpha_0 > 0\) and \(\alpha_i, \beta_i, \gamma_i \ge 0\). The GARCH and GJR-GARCH models are fitted with \(p = q = 1\). The persistence is denoted as \(\rho = \alpha + \beta\) for GARCH(1,1) and for a GJR-GARCH with a symmetric \(D\): \(\rho = \alpha + \beta + \gamma/2\). If \(\rho < 1\) the variance process of the series is stationary. The unconditional variance is defined as \(\alpha_0/(1-\rho)\), and the half-life of a volatility shock is \(\log(0.5)/\log(\rho)\).
The three models above are compared to a constant variance model, \(\sigma_t^2 = s^2\), where \(s\) denotes the sample variance as well as EWMA with \(\sigma_t^2 = 0.94\,\sigma_{t-1}^2 + 0.06\,\varepsilon_{t-1}^2\), a GARCH(1,1) with \(\omega = 0\), \(\alpha + \beta = 1\) and no parameters estimated.
All ARCH and GARCH models are estimated by maximum likelihood using the rugarch package.



Conditional variance models consist of both a mean and variance equation. The conditional mean must be modelled before modelling the volatility. Returns are modelled using the best ARIMA model to capture any predictable structure in the mean. The residuals of the ARIMA model represent the shocks, \(\varepsilon_t\). Any autocorrelation left unexplained by the mean model would distort the variance model fitted to the residuals. An ARIMA model assumes constant variance and Engle’s (1982) LM test is used to test if this assumption holds. A small p-value rejects the null hypothesis of no ARCH effect, suggests volatility clustering and justifies an ARCH/GARCH model.

# Function to calculate the negative log-likelihood of a Gaussian GARCH(1,1)
# with a constant mean: 
garch11_nll_fxn = function(par, r) {
  mu    = par[1]
  omega = par[2] # this is alpha0 in notes 
  alpha = par[3]
  beta  = par[4]
  
  # Check: return a very large value if the parameter constraints are broken:
  if (omega <= 0 || alpha < 0 || beta < 0 || alpha + beta >= 1) {
    return(1e10)
  }
  
  # Calculate shocks:
  e = r - mu
  
  # Initialise: 
  n     = length(r)
  s2    = numeric(n)
  s2[1] = mean((r - mean(r))^2)
  
  # For loop to calculate the conditional variance: 
  for (t in 2:n) {
    s2[t] = omega+alpha*e[t-1]^2+beta*s2[t-1]
  }
  
  # Calculate negative log-likelihood:
  # optim minimises -> minimise -loglik:
  nll = 0.5*sum(log(2*pi)+log(s2)+e^2/s2)
  return(nll)
}

Since true variance is unobservable, volatility forecasts have to be compared with a noisy proxy, the squared return. Following Patton (2011), forecasts are compared using QLIKE, \(\text{QLIKE} = \log h_t + \hat\varepsilon_t^2 / h_t\), a loss function designed for noisy variance proxies. This metric is less affected by extreme days making it more reliable than MSE.
Table 8 reports the average MSE and QLIKE loss of each model’s one-day-ahead variance forecasts over the test set. The GJR-GARCH-\(t\) model has the lowest score on both measures (QLIKE = 0.805, MSE = 2.617). This is in agreement with the model chosen by BIC on the training set. When comparing models based on QLIKE, the constant-variance model performs the worst (1.063), providing evidence that the volatility of ALSI returns is predictable. The pure ARCH model slightly outperforms EWMA with QLIKE scores of 0.840 and 0.849 respectively. EWMA is a restricted GARCH(1,1) with no constant and fixed parameters (\(\alpha = 0.06\), \(\beta = 0.94\)), so it has no long-run variance to revert to. Both of these models perform worse than GARCH-N and GARCH-\(t\) (0.826 and 0.825). The addition of asymmetry yields the greatest improvement (0.805).
MSE ranks EWMA slightly above GARCH-N and GARCH-t (2.646 compared to 2.653 and 2.647). However, the differences are very small and MSE is more affected by extreme absolute returns, so the models are ranked according to QLIKE.
Figure 6 displays the one-day-ahead volatility forecasts of the constant-variance model, EWMA and GJR-GARCH-\(t\) for the test set. The annualised absolute returns are shown in grey. The constant model is just a flat line, underpredictng when returns spike and over predicting when returns drop. Both EWMA and GJR-GARCH-\(t\) rise sharply after large returns and decay slowly, this is indicative of the high persistence estimated earlier. In calm periods, EWMA drops lower than GJR-GARCH-\(t\) since it has no long-run variance to revert to. GJR-GARCH-\(t\) rises more after large drop then EWMA, due to the inclusion of the leverage effect.

Time series is a single measurement taken at multiple points across time. Technically we are modelling the same thing over and over again (this makes sense as to why there is sequential correlation).

Figure 1 plots the number of monthly airline passengers over a 12 year period. This figure clearly illustrates the concepts of seasonality and trend.
Example: Discrete series

Figure 2 plots the changing number of observed seals over a period of 25 years.
What to do when you have missing observations in a time series?
In discrete time series to deal with missing observations you can express the model in state-space form (ARIMA or Structural Time Series). For a missing observation \(y_t\), skip the update step in the kalman filter and only run the prediction step. The likelihood is evaluated only over the observed time points.






Kalman filtering



Kalman filtering (linear quadratic estimation) is an algorithm that uses a series of measurements over time to estimate unknown variables, by estimating a joint probability distribution over the variables for each time-step.


In continuous time series, missing observations look like irregularly spaced sampling intervals. You can model the underlying system using Stochastic Differential Equations (CARMA) or you can aggregate the irregular time steps into regular, discrete intervals.



Aggregating up can either smooth out high-frequency structure (stock returns, etc) or can reveal low-frequency structure (Sales, etc).



Noise in the data introduces different realisations. If your model fits one dataset perfectly then it is overfitting.

title: Predicting drought in the Western Cape
text:
Figure 16: 2-year forecasts of Theewaterskloof dam capacity using a SARIMA(2,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] model.




Figure 16 shows the forecast using SARIMA(2,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] on the dam levels series through 2026 and 2027. The strong seasonal cycle is maintained although the forecasted peaks are slightly lower than the previous few years. The model is reverting back towards more typical levels as opposed to just extrapolating the most recent observations. The uncertainty associated with these forecasts grows substantially with the forecast horizon. Since this model is built on its own history with no covariate added it cannot predict the onset of an El Niñoevent nor drought in the Western Cape.








Figure 17: 2-year forecasts of eastern Pacific sea surface temperature using an AR(1,0,0)(0,1,0)[12] model.




Figure 17 shows the forecast using AR(1,0,0)(0,1,0)[12] on the sea surface temperature series through 2022 and 2023. The series maintains its strong seasonal pattern with temperatures peaking around 26°C and dropping to approximately 22°C. This is similar to the historical pattern. Uncertainty in the prediction intervals grows with the forecast horizon but not as much as for the dam level series. The prediction only extends into 2023 since the model was built on pre-2021 data due to large portions of missing observations after 2021. A simple AR process is unable to predict unprecedented events as the model forecasts revert towards typical seasonal values. Even if the model was forecasting into 2027 it would be unable to pick up the anticipated 2026/2027 El Niñoevent.

title: Predicting drought in the Western Cape
text:
The optimal model for the Theewaterskloof dam capacity series is the SARIMA(2,0,0)(0,1,1)[12] model. This model was selected based on the PACF plot in Figure 12 as well as a comparison of its error metrics with the initial SARIMA model specification. For sea surface temperature, Figure 12’s PACF plot suggested that SST prediction would not be improved by a more complex seasonal model. This was confirmed when the AR(1,0,0)(0,1,0)[12] model, on average, outperformed all other candidate models, when their error metrics were compared. Using SST as a lagged predictor for dam capacity was statistically insignificant as it did not improve predictive accuracy beyond what the series history already did.



There were several limitations when working with these datasets. The structural gaps present in the SST series (November 2021 - March 2023, October 2024 - March 2025) meant that the regression analysis could only use pre-2021 data. This loss of information decreased the size of the training set and meant that the model could not predict into 2027, when the super El Niñois anticipated.
The CCF-derived 6 month lag is consistent with the typical literature-motivated 3-6 month window for El Nino, however, the CCF is dominated by the common 12-month seasonality of both the series rather than a clean lead-lag signal. Thus, it cannot be accurately determined if a 6 month lag is the true lag.



To predict drought in the Western Cape, it would be more useful to use rainfall data as this has a direct impact on dam levels. Monitoring water usage across the country may also provide improved predictive information that eastern Pacific sea surface temperature.
The structural gaps in the SST data could be worked around by using a more comprehensive set of buoy observations that span a wider longitudinal range than the single 95W array used here. By replacing the buoy array with an array that averages over a larger region of the Pacific, there would be fewer missing observations and the series would not need to be truncated to avoid large structural gaps. The El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO) moves through El Nino, La Niña and neutral periods. It may be useful to use a regime-switching model that would capture this variability as opposed to a model with fixed coefficients.

title: Predicting the volatility of daily Johannesburg Stock Exchange All Share Index returns
text:
The financial series used is the daily FTSE/JSE All Share Index total return index \(P_t\) (ticker J203, dividends reinvested) over the period from 30 June 1995 to 3 February 2017. The time index used is “trading day” since weekends are excluded. The daily log returns (%) are modelled,
\[
r_t = 100[lnP_t - lnP_{t-}].
\] Log returns are modelled since asset prices wander and their variance grows without bound. The series consists of 5396 total daily returns. The models are estimated using the training set (July 1995 - December 2012) and evaluated on the test set (January 2013 - February 2017).

# Function to calculate summary statistics:
summary_fxn = function(x){
  n            = length(x)               # no. observations
  avg          = mean(x)                 # Average returns

  min_         = min(x)                  # Minimum

              sd=sd,

title: Predicting the volatility of daily Johannesburg Stock Exchange All Share Index returns
text:
Conditional variance models consist of both a mean and a variance equation:
\[
r_t = \mu_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \qquad z_t \overset{iid}{\sim} D(0,1),
\]
where \(\mu_t=\mu+\phi r_{t-1}\), \(\sigma_t^2\) is the conditional variance and \(D\) is the standard normal or a standardised Student-\(t\) distribution with \(\nu\) degrees of freedom.
In the ARCH model, the conditional variance depends on past squared shocks. The GARCH model lets the conditional variance depend on its own past as well as on past squared shocks. The GJR-GARCH model is a threshold model that captures the asymmetric leverage effect, where negative shocks increase volatility more than positive shocks of the same magnitude.







Model
Conditional variance \(\sigma_t^2\)




ARCH(\(q\))
\(\alpha_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{q}\alpha_i\varepsilon_{t-i}^2\)


GARCH(\(p,q\))
\(\alpha_0 + \sum^q_{i=1} \alpha_i \varepsilon_{t-i}^2 + \sum^p_{j=1} \beta_j \sigma_{t-j}^2\)


GJR-GARCH(\(p,q\))
\(\alpha_0 + \sum^q_{i=1} (\alpha_i + \gamma_iI_{t-i})\varepsilon^2_{t-i} + \sum^p_{j=1}\beta_j \sigma_{t-j}^2\), where \(I_{t-i} = 1\) if \(\varepsilon_{t-i} < 0\) and \(0\) otherwise



with \(\alpha_0 > 0\) and \(\alpha_i, \beta_i, \gamma_i \ge 0\). The GARCH and GJR-GARCH models are fitted with \(p = q = 1\). The persistence is denoted as \(\rho = \alpha + \beta\) for GARCH(1,1) and for a GJR-GARCH with a symmetric \(D\): \(\rho = \alpha + \beta + \gamma/2\). If \(\rho < 1\) the variance process of the series is stationary. The unconditional variance is defined as \(\alpha_0/(1-\rho)\), and the half-life of a volatility shock is \(\log(0.5)/\log(\rho)\).
The three models above are compared to a constant variance model, \(\sigma_t^2 = s^2\), where \(s\) denotes the sample variance as well as EWMA with \(\sigma_t^2 = 0.94\,\sigma_{t-1}^2 + 0.06\,\varepsilon_{t-1}^2\), a GARCH(1,1) with \(\omega = 0\), \(\alpha + \beta = 1\) and no parameters estimated.
All ARCH and GARCH models are estimated by maximum likelihood using the rugarch package.

title: Predicting the volatility of daily Johannesburg Stock Exchange All Share Index returns
text:
Conditional variance models consist of both a mean and variance equation. The conditional mean must be modelled before modelling the volatility. Returns are modelled using the best ARIMA model to capture any predictable structure in the mean. The residuals of the ARIMA model represent the shocks, \(\varepsilon_t\). Any autocorrelation left unexplained by the mean model would distort the variance model fitted to the residuals. An ARIMA model assumes constant variance and Engle’s (1982) LM test is used to test if this assumption holds. A small p-value rejects the null hypothesis of no ARCH effect, suggests volatility clustering and justifies an ARCH/GARCH model.


Code
# Parameter grid:
arima_grid = expand_grid(p=0:2,q=0:2)  # Test different arma models

# Function to fit multiple ARIMA models:
arima_fxn = function(dat,p,q) {
  fit = arima(dat,order=c(p,0,q),method="ML")
  tibble(`ARIMA(p,d,q)`  = paste0("(",p,",0,",q,")"),
         loglik =as.numeric(logLik(fit)),
         AIC    = AIC(fit),
         BIC    = BIC(fit))
}
  
arima_res = arima_grid |>
  pmap(\(p,q) arima_fxn(r_train,p,q)) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  arrange(BIC)

# Function to calculate the negative log-likelihood of a Gaussian GARCH(1,1)
# with a constant mean: 
garch11_nll_fxn = function(par, r) {
  mu    = par[1]
  omega = par[2] # this is alpha0 in notes 
  alpha = par[3]
  beta  = par[4]
  
  # Check: return a very large value if the parameter constraints are broken:
  if (omega <= 0 || alpha < 0 || beta < 0 || alpha + beta >= 1) {
    return(1e10)
  }
  
  # Calculate shocks:
  e = r - mu
  
  # Initialise: 
  n     = length(r)
  s2    = numeric(n)
  s2[1] = mean((r - mean(r))^2)
  
  # For loop to calculate the conditional variance: 
  for (t in 2:n) {
    s2[t] = omega+alpha*e[t-1]^2+beta*s2[t-1]
  }
  
  # Calculate negative log-likelihood:
  # optim minimises -> minimise -loglik:
  nll = 0.5*sum(log(2*pi)+log(s2)+e^2/s2)
  return(nll)
}

With over 4000 observations, even small autocorrelations become statistically significant. Figure 5 illustrates the small remaining autocorrelations in comparison to those in @fig (reference EDA plot here), showing that most of the volatility clustering has been removed.

This shows that most of the heavy tails can be attributed to volatility clustering. The remaining excess kurtosis is close to that of a Student-\(t\) distribution with \(\hat\nu \approx 10\) degrees of freedom, \(6/(\nu - 4) \approx 1.0\), which supports the Student-\(t\) innovations. This is confirmed by the QQ-plot in Figure 5 where the points like on the diagonal except for a few extreme negative returns.

Following Patton (2011), forecasts are compared using QLIKE, \(\text{QLIKE} = \log h_t + \hat\varepsilon_t^2 / h_t\), a loss function designed for noisy variance proxies. This metric is less affected by extreme days making it more reliable than MSE.

The GJR-GARCH-\(t\) model has the lowest score on both measures (QLIKE = 0.805, MSE = 2.617). This is in agreement with the model chosen by BIC on the training set. When comparing models based on QLIKE, the constant-variance model performs the worst (1.063), providing evidence that the volatility of ALSI returns is predictable. The pure ARCH model slightly outperforms EWMA with QLIKE scores of 0.840 and 0.849 respectively. Figure 6 displays the one-day-ahead volatility forecasts of the constant-variance model, EWMA and GJR-GARCH-\(t\) for the test set. The annualised absolute returns are shown in grey. The constant model is just a flat line, underpredictng when returns spike and over predicting when returns drop. Both EWMA and GJR-GARCH-\(t\) rise sharply after large returns and decay slowly, this is indicative of the high persistence estimated earlier. In calm periods, EWMA drops lower than GJR-GARCH-\(t\) since it has no long-run variance to revert to.
